headline: Karnataka Bitcoin scam: SIT issues new notice to Youth Congress chief Mohammed Haris
description: Mohammed Haris and his brother Omar Haris were previously questioned over their association with hacker Srikrishna Ramesh alias Sriki.
content:
The Special Investigation Team (SIT) of the Karnataka Criminal Investigation Department (CID) probing the Bitcoin scam has issued a fresh notice to state Youth Congress chief Mohammed Haris Nalapad to participate in the probe, according to CID sources.
Mohammed Haris, 34, and his brother Omar Haris, 29, were earlier questioned over two days in June 2024 over payments made by them for expenses incurred by hacker Srikrishna Ramesh alias Sriki, including his stay at luxury hotels, his travel and other expenses during the 2017 to 2018 period. They are the sons of Congress MLA N A Haris, the chairman of the Bangalore Development Authority.
The notice to Mohammed Nalapad comes at a time when the SIT is reported to be in the process of finalising two chargesheets in the Bitcoin scam about the involvement of police officers in destroying evidence and the alleged embezzlement of cryptocurrency from Sriki after his arrest in November 2020.
The SIT, which is probing alleged police corruption in the original handling of the hacking cases of the hacker following his arrest, is also looking at instances of possible usage of stolen cryptocurrency by the hacker in association with several high-profile friends from 2017 to 2023.
STORIES YOU MAY LIKE
After Delhi election, lesson for all parties: Listen to the ground
What former Delhi CMs Arvind Kejriwal, Atishi said as Rekha Gupta to take Delhi’s reins
Nita Ambani chooses Ranbir Kapoor over Ranveer Singh and Bill Gates, says, ‘He’s my son Akash’s best friend’. Watch
The SIT began its investigation into the Bitcoin scam in June 2023. Last year, the SIT filed a chargesheet against Sriki and his accountant Robin Khandelwal in connection with the hacking of Unocoin Technology Pvt Ltd’s crypto exchange in Karnataka that occurred on June 23, 2017. This incident resulted in the theft of 60.6 Bitcoins, which were valued at Rs 1.14 crore based on the prevailing rate of Rs 1.67 lakh per Bitcoin at that time.
Links of hacker to Mohammed Haris
Statements made to the police by Khandelwal, a Bitcoin trader based in Kolkata who also served as a crypto fund manager, suggested a connection between the Nalapad brothers and the hacker. These statements were provided following Khandelwal’s arrest by the Bengaluru crime branch police in November 2020. Khandelwal reported that he travelled to Bengaluru in 2018. This trip followed his online meeting with Sriki, during which he conducted several cryptocurrency trades on Sriki’s behalf.
During the visit to Bengaluru in January 2018, Khandelwal reported meeting Sriki at a five-star hotel with his friends, including Mohammad Nalappad, Omar Nalapad and their associate Mohammed Nafi, among others, as per the voluntary statement.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
“At this time, Srikrishna had hacked the databases of Bitcoin exchanges and kept a lot of Bitcoins with him. He showed me the Unocoin database,” as per Khandelwal’s statement.
In February 2018, Mohammed Nalapad was arrested following a brawl at a pub in central Bengaluru. During this incident, Srikrishna, who was with him, allegedly fled the city and reportedly with his fund manager in Kolkata and other locations.
There is no record of direct financial transactions between the hacker and the Nalapad brothers, including their fund manager. However, the hacker stated to the CID police in 2021, following his arrest for a hacking incident at the Karnataka government’s e-procurement portal in July 2019 that resulted in a ₹11.5 crore heist, that he had made an “investment” of 150 Bitcoin and 1,100 Ethereum with Mohammed Nalapad after meeting the brothers in 2017.
Police sources earlier reported that Srikrishna claimed he would give away the cryptocurrency he possessed to certain associates. However, those named by the hacker have denied these claims. According to the sources, the statements made by Srikrishna are currently being investigated and verified.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Several politicians and officials in Karnataka had their sons and relatives allegedly associated with Sriki between 2017 and 2020. Many reportedly used his hacking skills for personal gain, particularly in online gambling and other hacking activities. A senior IPS officer’s son was questioned by the SIT last year regarding his involvement in the purchase of a Porsche Macan car worth Rs 57 lakh by a group of youths. The funds for this were provided by Khandelwal in January 2018.
SIT sources indicated that the investigation into the hacker cases is in the final stages, with chargesheets being prepared for two cases registered in September 2023 and January 2024 against police officers and others. They said the SIT is seeking government approval to prosecute four police officers who were arrested in the case last year.
The Bitcoin scam: A timeline
Following his arrest in November 2020, Sriki claimed to the police that he had hacked multiple international exchanges between 2016 and 2020 and used stolen Bitcoin to lead a lavish lifestyle with his associates. He also alleged that he handed over a large cache of cryptocurrency in his possession to police officials after his arrest.
In response to allegations of large-scale corruption involving crime branch policemen and political leaders regarding the handling of the hacker’s cases during the 2019-2023 tenure of the BJP government in Karnataka, the newly formed Congress government established the SIT in June 2023 after coming to power in May 2023.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Over the past year, several police officers who were part of the Bengaluru crime branch during 2020-2021 have been investigated by the SIT. Four officers and a cyber expert who assisted the police in probing the hacker’s cases have been arrested for wrongdoing.
Based on statements from witnesses who aided the investigation in 2020, the SIT argued for the denial of bail to two police officers accused in the scam, stating that the hacker Sriki was in possession of over 4,000 Bitcoins, valued at approximately Rs 850 crore, at the time of his arrest in November 2020.
Srikrishna and his accountant Khandelwal were initially arrested by the Bengaluru crime branch in November 2020 on charges of purchasing drugs online using Bitcoin. This case involving drug purchases on the darknet ultimately led to the uncovering of several cyber crimes in Karnataka, including a Rs 11.5 crore fund heist from the Karnataka e-governance cell in 2019.
At the time of the hacker’s arrest in 2020, the value of one Bitcoin was in the range of $20,000 (around Rs 20 lakh), and it surged to as high as $50,000 (around Rs 50 lakh) by April 2021. The value of one Bitcoin recently hit $1,00,000.

headline: Karnataka government nurse uses Fevikwik adhesive to close boy’s wound, suspended
description: The incident was reported at a PHC in Adoor village of Haveri district on January 14; the suspended nurse defends her action.
content:
A government staff nurse in Karnataka was suspended on Wednesday for allegedly using Fevikwik, an instant adhesive, instead of medical stitches to close the facial wound of a seven-year-old boy.
The incident was reported at a Primary Health Centre (PHC) in Adoor village of Haveri district on January 14.
The suspended staff nurse Jyothi, when questioned by the boy’s parents, defended her action stating that if stitches are used, the marks would remain on cheeks.
The parents had posted the alleged act of the nurse on social media after the wound of the child worsened, prompting the Health and Family Welfare Department to suspend Jyothi for dereliction of duty.
“Fevikwik is an adhesive solution not permitted for medical use under regulations. In this case, the staff nurse responsible for dereliction of duty by using Fevikwik for the child’s treatment has been suspended following a preliminary report and pending further investigation as per rules,” Commissioner’s Office of Health and Family Welfare department said in a statement.
The authorities have been directed to monitor if there are any adverse effect caused by Fevikwik on the child, said the department.
The parents of the child rushed him to the primary health centre after he injured his cheek while playing.

The condition of the child is reported to be stable, the health authorities said.

headline: ‘Dreamed of better life… was treated like criminal in detention centre’: Parents of Gujarati native deportee from the US
description: The 29-year-old woman’s family welcomed her with teary eyes, expressing joy that their daughter was ‘back home safe’
content:
The presence of the district police teams, mediapersons, and curious onlookers outside the house of a 29-year-old woman’s family from Padra taluka in Vadodara district has left the family flustered.
On Thursday morning, the woman returned to her village home — following her deportation, with 103 other Indians, in a US military aircraft that arrived in Amritsar on Wednesday.
Her family welcomed her with teary eyes, expressing joy that their daughter was “back home safe.”
“We were tense and worried… all through the time, she was out of touch. As far as we know, she did nothing illegal. We do not know what went wrong. We were out of touch for several days and it was only the day before that we heard about her return,” said her mother.
Her father, a farmer, said, “We are a simple family. She had dreamed of a better life and initiated the process accordingly… We do not know what went wrong. We have welcomed her home and there is no question of attempting to go again. We will keep her with us.”
The father added that the woman, who was one of 33 deported Gujarati natives who had reached Ahmedabad in the aircraft, was “traumatised”.
“She has been crying since she was able to contact us from the detention centre where the Indians were kept for a few days. They were not given access to communication and we had not heard from her… they were treated like criminals. We will ensure she recovers from this mental state of mind,” he said.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
The woman, who was escorted by a team of the Vadodara district police from the Ahmedabad airport was “handed over” to her family at the Padra police station on Thursday morning.
Vadodara District Superintendent of Police, Rohan Anand, told The Indian Express, “We had received an intimation that they (deportees) were coming from New Delhi… We dispatched a team of the district police to bring her back safely. We have not questioned her right now and once she settles, we will approach her.”

headline: Court highlights flaws in police theory: ‘The way in which raid has been conducted… speaks a lot about doubt in the prosecution case’
description: The court of Additional District and Sessions Judge (ADSJ) Ajit Attri acquitted Sarabjeet Singh, Deepak Kumar, Rajni Vinayak and Atika Sikka on January 27.
content:
The district court has acquitted four persons, including two women, in a case relating to selling counterfeit currency notes. The court highlighted the flaws in the police theory after the defence alleged in the trial that all the persons acquitted were falsely implicated in the case to get a house vacated which belongs to the mother of a senior police officer.
The court of Additional District and Sessions Judge (ADSJ) Ajit Attri acquitted Sarabjeet Singh, Deepak Kumar, Rajni Vinayak and Atika Sikka on January 27. The detailed judgment was uploaded on February 4.
While acquitting all the accused, the court observed, “It is held that the prosecution has failed to prove the offence under sections 120-B (criminal conspiracy), 420 (cheating), 489- A (whoever counterfeits, or knowingly performs any part of the process of counterfeiting), 489-B (whoever sells to, or buys or receives from, any other person, or otherwise traffics in or uses as genuine, any forged or counterfeit currency-note), 489-C (Whoever has in his possession any forged or counterfeit currency-note), and 489-D (Whoever has in his possession any forged or counterfeit currency-note) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for which the accused were charged, beyond reasonable doubt and the accused Sarabjeet Singh, Deepak Kumar, Rajni Vinayak and Atika Sikka are acquitted of the charges framed against them by giving them benefit of doubt.”
The prosecution case was that on July 17, 2021, secret informer informed SI (Sub-Inspector) Manpreet Singh that Sarabjeet Singh, who was representing himself to be a police officer, along with Rajni Vinayak, alias Khaira Madam, Deepak Kumar, Atika Sikka and other unknown persons in connivance with each other are indulging in the business of selling fake Indian currency notes.
They prepare these currency notes by themselves and ask the people that whatever amount of original currency notes they will give them, they will double the amount of fake currency notes and these can be used in the market as the real currency notes.
They are also using these fake currency notes in the market as real currency notes and if raid would be conducted, they could be apprehended with fake currency notes and mechanical and electrical instruments used for preparing fake currency notes could be recovered. On the basis of the above said secret information, FIR was registered.
Thereafter, a raid was conducted at their house and from one room, 20 currency notes of the denomination of Rs 500 and 10 currency notes of the denomination of Rs 200 amounting to Rs 12,000 were recovered from accused Rajni Vinayak and Atika Sikka.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
While highlighting the flaws in the investigation of the case, the court noted, “It is the case of the accused right from the stage of bail application that in fact accused Atika Sikka had taken House No.44, Phase 3-A, Mohali on rent, which was in the name of the mother of the senior police official at Mohali and they wanted to get it vacated and accused Atika Sikka had also initiated civil suit for permanent injunction against the owner of the said house as well as others, who were police officials for threatening her and to get the house vacated illegally without following due procedure of law.”
“But the IO as well as other officials involved in the investigation, remained oblivious of this fact, though it is coming on the record from the initial stage. The IO, who is also complainant of the case, made an effort to depose with said precision that case will look full proof, but the way and manner in which raid has been conducted and further investigation has been conducted by PW-4 that itself speaks a lot about the doubt in the case of the prosecution with regard to the said raid,” the court observed.
Noting further, the court observed, “It is the case of the prosecution in the evidence of PW-4 (SI Manpreet Singh) as well as in the evidence of PW-2 (Inspector Ravinder Singh) who was member of the police party at the time of raid that the police party first entered the ground floor where accused Atika Sikka and Rajni Vinayak were found and fake currency has also been recovered while lying on the bed.”
“PW-4 as well as PW-2 have specifically deposed that first they apprehended and recovered fake currency notes at the ground floor from the accused Atika Sikka and Rajni Vinayak and thereafter, they went to the first floor of the house, where accused Deepak Kumar was found operating on the laptop.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
If it was not the raid simultaneously on the entire house, then it cannot be believed that accused Deepak Kumar, who was said to be working at that time on the computer, will not come to know and will keep waiting for the police party to come in his room and apprehend him and recover the currency notes. It is not the case of the prosecution that it is multi-storey building, rather as per information, which is made out from the case, there are ground floor and first floor in the said house,” the court highlighted.
On the house in question, the court observed, “If the IO PW-4 is taken as per his deposition, the secret informer when met second time, he had even told about accused Deepak Kumar on the first floor and machinery installed on the first floor. In these circumstances, it does not stand to reason that the police party at the first instance will confine to ground floor only. In the cross-examination, PW-4 has stated that during investigation, he had found that owner of the House No. 44, Phase-3A, Mohali was Paramjit Kaur, wife of Swaran Singh, but he did not join Paramjit Kaur as witness in the present case.”
“He did not give any notice to said Paramjit Kaur to verify that she is owner of the house or whether she had let out the house to Atika Sikka, Rajni Vinayak and Deepak Kumar. He had not joined any of the neighbors to ascertain as to whether the accused were living in House No.44, Phase-3A, Mohali as tenants. PW-4 does not know whether son of Paramjit Kaur was the SSP of Mohali at that time. He had not called the owner of the said house at the time of preparing the site plan from where the recovery was effected by him,” the court observed.
“When the defence asked PW-4 with regard to the civil litigation initiated by accused against the owner of the said house and other police officials by making them party by name, PW-4 has shown his complete unawareness and ignorance. He has specifically stated that he did not have knowledge as to whether any civil litigation is going on in Mohali courts regarding the house in question or that stay had been granted by the Civil Court in favour of accused Atika Sikka,” the court remarked.

headline: Talks, protests, PILs: How resistance to Riverfront Development project flows through Pune
description: In the second part of a series of reports, The Indian Express looks at the opposition to the Pune Riverfront Development (RFD) project from various corners.
content:
On the afternoon of February 9, thousands of people are expected to converge at the Ram-Mula river confluence in Pune’s Baner for a Chipko march under the tagline “Save Trees, Save Rivers”. This is the latest iteration of a public movement against the Riverfront Development (RFD) project in Pune. The RFD undertaken by the Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) aims to rejuvenate the 44-km stretch of Mula and Mutha rivers passing through the city.
Marches are the most visible form of resistance, but the movement against the RFD also involves civil society members talking to the PMC. “Rather than protesting, we started discussions with the authorities about our reservations regarding the RFD. This was around 2018-19. Instead of saying no to the RFD, we said it could be implemented better on the river,” says Shailaja Deshpande of Jeevitnadi, a volunteer-based organisation involved in the protests.
“We still feel that the RFD can be an ecological riverfront that uses certain bio-engineering methods. Because the landscape changes in the urban areas drastically with time, there has to be a model where we compromise certain natural elements but not to an extent that will endanger the ecosystem,” adds Deshpande.
Legal challenges against Riverfront Development project
Protests against the RFD unfold over multiple levels, from engaging the administration to marches to filing environment interest litigations (EIL) at the National Green Tribunal (NGT). At present, there is a public interest litigation (PIL) before the Bombay High Court against the illegal demarcation of flood lines in Pune city development plan maps.
Sarang Yadwadkar is among those who have taken the resistance to the courts. In January, he knocked on the doors of the NGT again, this time against the environmental clearance given by the State Environment Impact Assessment Authority to the RFD.
“As far as the RFD is concerned, we need to understand the situation in Pune. It is very peculiar compared to any other city. Five rivers enter the city: Mula, Mutha, Pavana, Ramnadi and Devnadi. The last two are relatively smaller rivers but bring in water quickly. Flash floods occur in both rivers. We have seven dams upstream that are nearby. There are four dams on the Mutha and one each on Mutha and Pawana, apart from the Kasarsai Dam,” says Yadwadkar.
Also Read | First part of series: Pune’s Riverfront Development project to accelerate despite public outcry
“If there is a cloudburst and these dams start releasing water, all that water will enter the city quickly, i.e. within one or two hours. All the rivers converge and, ultimately, have only one outlet: the Mula Mutha River. So, our city is at the neck of the funnel. Water enters from five different catchments, and there is only one outlet. That is a very dangerous position; as if we are sitting on a live bomb,” he adds.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
In 2019, when the Ambil Odha, which is a tributary, suffered from a flash flood, around 25 people died. There was destruction to property, including houses. “Because all these rivers and their tributaries originate from the Sahyadris, their catchments are very steep. Only once the water enters the city do the rivers start flowing relatively slowly. The water enters the city very fast but flows out slowly, which further increases this risk,” he adds.
Delhi-based The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) has projected an annual increase in rainfall in Pune by 10-37.5 per cent between the 2030s and 2070s. It predicted that the annual rainfall would rise, but the number of rainy days would also decrease.
“This could lead to more frequent occurrences of cloudburst events. If there is more traffic on roads, urban planners decide to widen the roads, so, if there is more water, why not widen the rivers?” asks Yadwadkar.
He adds, “Instead of widening, the RFD is narrowing the rivers by 40 per cent by dumping truckloads of debris in the river. Any reduction in the width will lead to erosion in the flood-carrying capacity of the river, which will result in more frequent and severe floods in Pune city in future.
Cosmetic surgery, allege critics of RFD
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
For several sceptics of the RFD plan, the issue is that the civic bodies are trying to decorate the river with concrete instead of prioritising cleaning the river. They are concerned about the fate of aquifers and existing biodiversity, among others. While several citizens are opposed only to implementing the RFD, Ameet Singh, an economist, is “completely against the project”.
Singh has fought the PMC before, particularly against tree felling on Ganeshkhind Road. Last year, the Bombay High Court instructed the PMC to stop cutting trees for road widening.
“The RFD is a blunder being perpetrated on Pune’s people by reclaiming Pune’s flood plains for a real estate grab and a 30-metre wide road. Over 1,600 acres will be reclaimed across 44 km of the river’s length. Lakhs of trees and riparian forests will be decimated, and over 41 crore sq ft of new real estate will be added to Pune’s already congested, polluted and broken urban infrastructure. If we can’t breathe clean air, drink pure water and live in a zero-garbage clean environment, what’s the point of this sort of development?” asks Singh.
He points out how “with the release of about 30,000 cusecs from Khadakwasla on July 25, 2024, the blue lines at most places in Pune were smudged and inundated with water”.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Singh says Maharashtra Engineering Research Institute now puts the water volume to be considered for redrawing the flood lines at 1,07,724 cusecs or almost double the volume of water from the older calculation, “There are increased incidences of huge urban flooding across Pune. Despite all of this, we continue to dump debris and concrete on the river bank and expect that Pune won’t flood,” he says.
Scientist and lawyer Rajendra Kumar Kale says the Mula-Mutha river system in Pune is highly polluted due to untreated sewage, industrial effluents, and other pollutants. “Yet, the project appears to prioritise real estate development and urban beautification over genuine ecological restoration. From my perspective, the critical issues with PMC’s river rejuvenation project include its focus on real estate development rather than actual river rejuvenation and neglect of pollution control,” he says.
Kale says the DPR proposes arresting sewage inflows near the rivers and diverting them to upcoming (and delayed) sewage treatment plants. “This approach risks legitimising the use of natural water streams as open sewage conduits. My argument is to achieve pollution-free rivers; the action must start at the source—by preventing sewage outfall into Pune’s 23 natural water streams. This is both logical and legally mandated,” says Kale.
“Recreational infrastructure should follow only after pollution is addressed. This approach has been successfully adopted in developed nations, such as Norway’s Akerselva river restoration project. Building recreational facilities around polluted rivers is neither logical nor sustainable,” adds Kale.

headline: ‘When deportees are from whole country, why was Amritsar chosen?’: In Punjab, questions raised over US flight landing in state
description: A United States military aircraft with 104 deported Indians landed in Punjab’s Amritsar, leading to speculation on whether it was a ‘face-saving move’ by the Centre.
content:
Hours after a United States military aircraft with 104 deported Indians landed in Punjab on Wednesday, state Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) president Aman Arora questioned why it landed in Amritsar and not any other airport in the country.
“When the deportees are from the whole country, why was Amritsar chosen as a location for landing the aircraft? This question is playing on everyone’s mind,” Arora told the media in Bathinda on Wednesday afternoon.
“The Centre has always given Punjab step-motherly treatment. People (deportees) from other states are more than those from Punjab. By leaving the national capital and choosing Amritsar for landing this aircraft, it raises a question mark,” Arora added.
The aircraft carried 104 Indians from Haryana, Gujarat, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Chandigarh. Sources said the highest number of deportees – 33 each – were from Gujarat and Haryana, followed by 30 from Punjab. Two deportees each are from Uttar Pradesh and Chandigarh, while three are from Maharashtra.
Nitin Chawla, director of Ludhiana-based Kapri Immigration Consultants, echoed Arora’s concerns. “Why was Amritsar chosen? I fail to understand. They could have landed at Delhi or any other international airport. Why is a narrative being set up against our state?” Chawla asked.
Ajaypal Singh Brar, the president of Ferozepur-based NGO Misl Satluj, condemned the deportation, saying that using a military aircraft like the C-17 — much more expensive than a civilian flight – was a deliberate attempt to humiliate India before Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to the US.
Brar also criticised the decision to land the flight in Amritsar, calling it a “face-saving move”. “Had the flight landed in the national capital, it would have been a major embarrassment for a government that claims to have strong ties with the US administration,” he said. “I feel that it is an effort to tarnish the image of Punjabis by falsely portraying them as the primary group involved in illegal immigration. Deported individuals belonged to various states across India, but the government and media are selectively pushing a narrative that unfairly targets Punjab,” he added.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Brar urged the youth in Punjab to avoid illegal immigration routes and instead focus on creating opportunities for themselves within the state through business and employment. He also criticised both the present and past governments for failing to provide meaningful jobs and a conducive environment for economic growth in Punjab, saying this has forced many youngsters to seek risky alternatives abroad.

headline: Narela to Karawal Nagar: A poll journey across Delhi’s 70 constituencies
description: New Delhi is perhaps the most heated battle in this Capital contest, as Delhi’s former Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal goes toe to toe with Congress’ Sandeep Dikshit (son of former Delhi CM Sheila Dikshit) and BJP's Parvesh Sahib Singh (son of Delhi’s former CM Sahib Singh Verma).
content:
As Delhi voted on Wednesday, The Indian Express travelled across the city, from constituency no. 1 (Narela) to constituency no. 70 (Karawal Nagar), and found that people voted for better roads, clean water, a remedy for pollution, garbage-free streets, and a compassionate government.
Sakshi Chand, Ankita Upadhyay, Gayathri Mani, Sohini Ghosh, Vidheesha Kuntamalla, Nirbhay Thakur, Upasika Singhal, Saman Husain, Pragynesh, Sophiya Mathew, Neetika Jha, Devansh Mittal & Ishfaq Bhat report.
New Delhi
It is 6.30 am. The heart of the Capital — comprising 1.09 lakh voters – is geared up for a big-ticket contest which will perhaps signal who will rule Delhi once results are declared on Saturday.
At polling station 44, near Sanchar Bhawan in the New Delhi constituency, stands a man in a grey sweater, with a chiseled face. He is in a hurry. “I believe the election this time will be very close. Some people want change. I’ve come early… couldn’t wait to vote,” says Desraj, 43.
Former Delhi CM and AAP national convener Arvind Kejriwal with his family after casting his vote at a polling booth during the Delhi Assembly elections. (Express Photo by Amit Mehra)
New Delhi is perhaps the most heated battle in this Capital contest, as Delhi’s former Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal goes toe to toe with Congress’ Sandeep Dikshit (son of former Delhi CM Sheila Dikshit) and BJP’s Parvesh Sahib Singh (son of Delhi’s former CM Sahib Singh Verma).
Also Read | Freebies or development — East Delhi divided
Two km away from Sanchar Bhawan is Nirman Bhawan – a polling station where 1,100 voters are registered. Among these voters are two big faces – Parvesh and Congress Leader and LoP Rahul Gandhi.
Outside polling booth in CR Park. (Express Photo by Gajendra Yadav)
For Akshat, 23, who voted for the first time at a polling station near a school in Laxmi Bai Nagar, pollution and lack of public transport are the main issues. “I wish there were more buses. A good public transport system is essential for Delhi. I also want to live in a pollution-free Delhi.”
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Nine kilometres away is C R Park in the Greater Kailash constituency, which has 13 polling stations. On the way to the stations which are in proximity to each other are various tables where polling agents belonging to the AAP and the BJP – the main rivals in this election – are sitting.

“We’ve been instructed by our party to check EVMs and their batteries… whether they’re fully charged or not,” says Chandan (41), a polling agent from AAP.
Also Read | Delhi exit polls: How accurate were they in the last three elections?
Chandni Chowk
Haiderpur and Shalimar villages in the Shalimar Bagh constituency are buzzing at 7.27 am. Officers from the Delhi Police and the Central Armed Police Force are on the ground, making sure everything is ready for voters.
Must Read | Delhi Assembly Elections: Most exit polls give BJP edge, AAP says never right
At 8 am, Sushma Malik (51), a differently abled woman, comes on her retrofitted scooter with her son Aryan Malik (19). Volunteers arrange a wheelchair and escort her inside. As she comes out, she says: “I voted for improvement. Better roads, better traffic, cleanliness.”
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Though many people say they are voting for ‘vikas (development)’ and ‘badlav (change)’, they also add they are satisfied with the current government.
Senior voters show their inked finger after casting a vote for the Delhi Assembly election. (Express Photo By Amit Mehra)
In the Adarsh Nagar Assembly constituency, a strong stench permeates the air at the Azadpur Sabzi Mandi. Residents in the area are linked to the sprawling market – either as vegetable shop owners, as workers or as retailers who buy from the wholesale market.
“Maine apna kartavya poora kiya (I fulfilled my duty),” says 72-year-old Umesh Prasad, a voter from the nearby Bharola village who runs a vegetable shop.
Also Read | Delhi Elections 2025 Voting LIVE Updates: AAP rejects exit polls results, says pollsters have ‘historically’ underestimated its performance
“Jo bhi sarkar bane bus nirdhan ko pareshan na karey (Whoever forms the government should not trouble the poor).”
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
While the poor demand compassion, residents of the upper and middle-income group in the posh colony of Model Town voted against freebies.
The sentiment also echoes in Hudson Lane, a part of the Timarpur assembly constituency, where many voters spoke about rising pollution levels.
Dr Ruchi Singh, a voter from the area, demands that whoever forms the government should bring improvement in the lives of the upper middle class as well. “We don’t want freebies, we want better roads and infrastructure.”
Northwest Delhi
From the narrow, potholed streets of rural Rithala to the landscaped, gated colonies of Rohini Sector 13, the contrast is stark.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
In Rithala’s Vijay Vihar Phase 1, the first thing that hits one is the smell of sewage wafting through the air, mingling with the dust kicked up by the movement of pedestrians and rickety two-wheelers. The narrow streets are riddled with potholes, some large enough to collect stagnant water from recent rains.
The polling booth at the government primary school — Dilli Rithala Prathmik Vidyalaya — is an old, unassuming structure.
Among the voters is Fatima Bhano, a 38-year-old mother of two, who stands outside the polling booth, visibly frustrated. Her name was missing from the voter list. “They’re asking me to go to Sector 4 to vote. How is that fair?” she asks.
For Bhano, inflation and high electricity bills are the primary issues. “Even in winter, when we barely use electricity, the bills are so high. How are we supposed to manage?”
Also Read | ‘Feel like Indians today’: Pak Hindu immigrants vote for first time after being granted citizenship under CAA
Despite her limited means, Bhano sends her children to private schools. “Government schools are in terrible condition. It’s all a show — they lie about schools being great, but they are not,” she says.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Down the road, 68-year-old Ameerka Devi, a housewife, has just cast her vote. She spoke of her struggles with accessing clean water: “The water here is not potable. I’ve been drinking it for years, and it’s caused stomach infections.”
As one leaves Rithala, the smell of sewage fades, giving way to the wide, clean streets of Rohini Sector 13. Here, gated communities with manicured parks and high-rise apartment complexes dominate the area.
Outside a booth, 43-year-old banker Jyoti Godara and 44-year-old army officer Abhishek Kumar share their disillusionment with the present government.
A first-time voter, 18-year-old Srishti Garg, disagrees. “I’m content with how things are here, but I do hope the government takes stronger action on issues like pollution,” says the law aspirant.
West Delhi
The polling station of Government Sarvodaya Kanya Vidyalaya (GSKV) no. 2 in Khyala village of Rajouri Garden constituency, labelled as ‘Model Polling Station’, is abuzz at 9.30 am.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Devender Singh (56) and his mother Charanjit Kaur (82) say one of the pressing issues for them this election is inflation. “The rest does not matter. This is an industrial area so we have electricity cuts for as long as four hours during summer. We have voted for every possible party in the past but we’ve also seen that there has been no change.”
At 12.30 pm in Tilak Nagar constituency’s Government Sarvodaya Bal Vidyalaya — polling station no.2 — the BJP polling agents say voting has been slow in the morning but will pick up soon.
The constituency also includes the Widow Colony, where survivors of the 1984 anti-Sikh riots reside. There is no Congress booth outside the station.
Atar Kaur, 65, who lived in Trilokpuri before the riots broke out, lost 15 members of her family, including her husband to the riots. “Humare aansu bas Modi ne hi poche (Only Modi dried our tears). Whatever little happened for us, was done by him,” she says.
At the SC reserved seat of Madipur, Hansraj Model School is an anomaly, with its voters from the upscale Punjabi Bagh extension.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Ruby Singh (56) and Gagan Kaur (32), both voters in the area, say air pollution is a talking point for them. “We go abroad and realise we are so far behind in every aspect — education, roads, cleanliness. Every time they impose GRAP-3 or GRAP-4 when pollution goes up, we are directly affected. This is no way to tackle pollution…”
Around 3 pm, in Vikaspuri constituency, only BJP polling agents remain outside the polling station of Government Co-Ed Senior Secondary School at Bakkarwala which has five polling booths.
Near Chanchal Park, Akash Singh, 28, an associate in a private firm, says there has been a decline in the popularity of AAP. “Water is free, but is unusable. I have my own home, but still pay the electricity bill.”
At 4.15 pm in Najafgarh constituency’s polling station, Green Valley School, which sees voters primarily from the Maksudabad Colony, the crowd has thinned out.
R P Sharma, 70, a retired central government employee, says the BJP has done well to choose a new candidate for the constituency — Neelam Pahalwan, instead of Kailash Gahlot, the former AAP MLA from the area who has joined the BJP.
Northeast Delhi
A road cuts Chandu Nagar and divides it into two assemblies. On one side is Adarsh Lakhpat Model Secondary School collecting votes for Karawal Nagar while on the other side stands New Sandhya Public Secondary School which collects votes for Mustafabad.
Both schools see a steady flow of voters from 7 am, growing as the hours tick away. The narrow bylanes on the Karwal Nagar side seemed to overflow with saffron pennants while the Mustafabad side looked barren of any party paraphernalia.
Deen Mohammad (59) and Hakim Mallick (54) are waiting for a friend to cast his vote on the Mustafabad side. They say they will vote for a party that has a chance to win. “There is no way Tahir (Hussain, AIMIM candidate and an accused in the riots conspiracy case) will win,” says Mohammad, explaining why he won’t vote for AIMIM.
Samira (29), who is standing nearby, can’t contain her indignation. “Main toh patang ko vote dungi (Well, I’ll vote for the kite, AIMIM’s poll symbol),” she says.
In Kamal Nagar, the Hindu-dominant area of Mustafabad, saffron flags and pennants flutter from the ramparts of almost every house. “Dekhiye swasthya aur shiksha zaruri hai lekin uss se pehle zinda rehna zaruri hai. Zinda rehne ke liye zaruri hai dharm (Look health and education are important but before that one must need to survive. To survive you need dharma),” says a voter, Shiv Kumar (50).
Around 4 km away, in Babarpur, 17-year-old Anmol Verma, a volunteer at the Sant Parmanand Public School, Mohanpuri, is helping a tired Trilochan Singh (79), who had difficulties walking, to cast his vote.
Singh is able to vote without delay while a queue persist otherwise as residents keep turning up. After casting his vote, he says, “Kejriwal has done a lot for schools, and health by setting up mohalla clinics, free electricity for 200 units. The Centre has also done some work. We have ration cards. But because of the BJP, bade logon ko zyada faida hua (rich people have benefited more).”
South Delhi
In Kalkaji, from where Chief Minister Atishi is going up against BJP’s Ramesh Bidhuri and Congress’s Alka Lamba, the streets have been swept clean. Polling agents draped in symbol-less scarves sit at their desks, urging residents to step out and vote. “We have worked very hard for the party, and we believe our candidate (Ramesh Bidhuri) should get a chance,” says Vandana Sethi, 58, a BJP polling agent.
Soon, Atishi arrives to cast her vote. The CM’s neighbour, Sunita Maini, 69 says, “My father was a kattar (staunch) Congressi who fought for India’s independence. He used to say even if a dog stood for Congress, we should vote for it. But now, that logic makes no sense. The work being done here — sanitation, water supply, healthcare, electricity — is good.”
Voter sentiments are mixed across constituencies. While some voted based on governance and services, others cast their ballots against inflation and economic concerns.
Outside Ambedkar Nagar’s Sona Modern Public School, Kulvir Singh, 51, an operations head at a corporate firm, is in deep discussion with a friend who is a Kendriya Vidyalaya principal. “Apart from freebies, economic well-being is necessary,” Singh says. The principal adds, “We looked at manifestos carefully and are voting for the one that aligns with our personal aspirations.”
At a booth near Sainik Farms, in Mehrauli constituency, where DMRC construction chokes the roads with dust and congestion, an irate voter, clad in a trendy jacket and sunglasses, rushes past, exasperated. “I will not be voting again — this was torturous!” she says, attributing her frustration to booth mismanagement.
As the day progresses and South Delhi’s constituencies approach the last leg of voting, urgency picks up. At the Mehrauli Dargah booth, Khatoon Bano reflects on her vote, shaped by the recent wave of demolitions that displaced many in her area. “We will vote, keeping this in mind,” she says.
East Delhi
In ‘jamna-paar’, the day began with light rain and voting picked up only around 10 am.
In Patparganj — where former Deputy Chief Minister Manish Sisodia is the outgoing MLA and is contesting this time from Jangpura – many claim due to increased anti-incumbency, change seems to be the buzzword.
AAP candidate Manish Sisodia shows his inked finger after casting a vote during the Delhi Assembly elections, at Daryaganj in New Delhi. (Express Photo By Amit Mehra)
Agrim Kulsheshta, 22, the first one to vote at Mayur Vihar pocket 3, polling booth number 99 and 100, says, “I cast my vote for change… Mayur Vihar houses a good number of developed apartments but the areas here lack development… As you step out of your house, you feel like you are in hell… from traffic jams to poisonous air, potholed roads…”
In line to cast his vote at Trilokpuri constituency, Dharmendra, a WiFi provider said, “We don’t have to point out anything because everything here is in the open… I would have voted for AAP if they had repaired something or at least provided a sewer connection… My vote has gone to the party that is thinking about the upliftment of Dalits.”
Trilokpuri, a reserved constituency, has a sizable migrant population settled from Theni and Tirunelveli districts of Tamil Nadu.
One of them, Annaveli (65), says, “I came here with a six-month toddler about 55 years ago from Tamil Nadu… Block 22 where a large number of Tamilians live faces a water crisis… Sometimes, we get stinking water… during the rain, water enters our home….”
Her friend, Pungavanam, says, “The entire block was settled by Indira Gandhi amma… We need more people like her and Jayalalithaa… Jhadu (AAP) party is also good but pensions don’t come on time…”
In Laxmi Nagar, where BJP is currently in power, Archit Gupta, who works at All India Radio said, “My vote has gone against freebies… I want fresh air, congestion-free roads and footpaths to walk…. hospitals and schools…”
In Shaheen Bagh which comes under Okhla constituency, Huma, a clinical psychologist, appreciated BJP’s promise of providing “free pregnancy kits and Rs 21,000 to pregnant women.”
“I feel this is a great scheme because the facilities for pregnant women in Delhi are not good… I feel if such a scheme is implemented, mothers, especially single mothers will get a lot of help…,” she says.
In the contentious Jangpura constituency, 80-year-old MK Tandon says: “I cast my vote at 8 am… I want a double-engine government this time. I have a reason because Manish Sisodia went to jail in a liquor scam and he held several portfolios… he did nothing… Roads are so poor in a posh area like this…”

headline: ‘No parks, no new infrastructure — my village has been the same for the past 15 years:’ At Delhi’s polling station No.1 in Lampur village, discontent simmers
description: From the seat, the AAP has fielded Dinesh Bharadwaj, replacing sitting MLA Sharad Kumar. The BJP has fielded Raj Karan Khatri and the Congress candidate is Aruna Kumari.
content:
Yellow barricades stand out amid wheat crops in Lampur, Delhi’s last village. A kilometre away on the other side is Haryana, where the sight of lush fields is far more common.
Located on the Northwestern edge of Delhi, the village falls under the Narela assembly constituency. On Wednesday, its government school, Nagar Nigam Prathmik (Co-ed) Utkrisht Vidyalaya, doubles up as polling station no. 1 as Delhi goes to polls.
From the seat, the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has fielded Dinesh Bharadwaj, replacing sitting MLA Sharad Kumar. The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has fielded Raj Karan Khatri and the Congress candidate is Aruna Kumari.
Outside the primary school, a group of farmers, dressed in woolen sweaters, discuss everything from crop yields to local politics as they wait to vote. Their conversations show a simmering discontent.
Pointing to the barricades, Prem Singh Saini, says, “Bas ek kilometre dur hai Haryana. Aur yahan humare halat dekh lo. (Haryana is just a kilometre away, but look at our condition here).” He is referring to better civic amenities across the border, as compared to Delhi.
The 65-year-old, who owns five acres of land, adds, “We’ve been facing immense losses because of unpredictable weather. There’s no insurance for vegetable crops. When a hailstorm destroyed my harvest two years ago, I received no help from the ruling AAP.”
The village, predominantly dominated by Sainis, is a picture of neglect with its crumbling infrastructure and glaring lack of development.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
“The roads are all broken,” says 49-year-old Anil Saini, who has lived in Lampur all his life. “AAP built a community hall here, but it’s been lying vacant for years. There are no parks, no new infrastructure. My village has been the same for the past 15 years.”
Navigating the pothole-riddled roads to reach the polling station, 55-year-old Choti Devi and her daughter-in-law Taravati could be seen covering their faces with their saree pallus. Taravati, 32, touched the feet of her elders before heading to vote. Her hopes, like those of many women in the village, rest on promises yet to be fulfilled.
“I enrolled in both the Mahila Samman Yojana by AAP and the Mahila Samridhi Yojana by BJP,” Taravati says. “Dono ka card bhara hai, dekhte hai ab konsa milega (I filled forms for both schemes; let’s see which one comes through).”
For Choti Devi, the lack of basic amenities overshadows any election rhetoric. “We haven’t been able to make ration cards for years, and no leader has helped us,” she says.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
“When it rains, the roads are impossible to travel on. And because we’re near the border, there are safety concerns too.”
Adjusting her pallu, she says with a resigned sigh, “Vote daal toh diye, ab sab bhagwan ke haath me (We’ve cast our votes; now everything is in God’s hands).”
The lack of a secondary school for girls in the village is another pressing issue. “Our girls have to go to another village to study. We want a school here so they can be safe,” Choti Devi says.
The frustration with the lack of development isn’t confined to roads and schools. Vimla Devi, 56, a housewife, points to the broken sewer lines in Dal Mill street. “All the sewers are open, and the sewage is flowing in the streets,” she says.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Like the others, she is disillusioned by the local leadership. “If no one listens to us this time, I won’t vote in the next election,” she insists. The farmers in the village are also frustrated by the lack of government support for their crops.
Ten km away is the Singhu border, a stark reminder of the year-long farmers’ protest between 2020 and 2021 when thousands of farmers, primarily from Punjab and Haryana, marched to Delhi to demand the repeal of three contentious agriculture laws.
For Lampur’s farmers, the protests symbolised hope — and eventual heartbreak.
“MSP hataoge toh kisaan fasal kaise ugaega?” asked Prem Singh, referring to the government’s minimum support price. “No party is truly listening to us.”
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Surender Saini, 58, who cultivates eight acres of wheat and vegetables, held a contrasting view. “Yeh aandolan bas rajneeti tha (the protests were all political). I’ve stopped paying attention because I’ve lost hope.” He adds that his earnings have dropped by Rs 1,000 per quintal compared to previous years.

headline: RG Kar corruption case: Parents seek time as HC weighs on reprobe
description: The state government, meanwhile, submitted a report asserting that it had “no role” in the investigation.
content:
The parents of the R G Kar Medical College and Hospital rape-murder victim have sought additional time from the Calcutta High Court regarding its decision to order a reinvestigation into the case.
Their counsel, Gargi Goswami, informed the court: “We had appealed to the Supreme Court asking whether the single bench of Calcutta High Court has the liberty to hear the matter. The matter will be heard this week in the Supreme Court; thus, we are praying for time.”
The state government, meanwhile, submitted a report asserting that it had “no role” in the investigation.

headline: Delhi Assembly elections: What voters say on voting day

content:
With Aam Aadmi Party facing off its INDIA bloc partner Congress and the BJP in a triangular contest, Delhi is voting on Wednesday to elect members for its 70-seat assembly, While the AAP is eyeing a third consecutive term in the government, the BJP and the Congress are looking to wrest its power from the ruling dispensation.

Even as all eyes are on the exit polls, that will be out once the polling is over, such surveys ever since AAP’s debut in 2013 have failed to capture the extent of the Arvind Kejriwal-led party’s dominance. While the average of exit polls correctly predicted a hung Assembly in 2013, they predicted much closer contests in 2015 and 2020, two elections in which the AAP nearly swept Delhi’s 70 Assembly seats. The Indian Express Wednesday spoke to a number of voters at various polling booths across the city to sense the pulse of the political battleground that the capital city has turned into. Here’s a look at what they said:

Shubham Mishra, 28, finance sector, Laxmi Nagar constituency
“I am going to vote for change. AAP has done nothing in Delhi to improve infrastructure. We get polluted water, pollution and there is always traffic jam in Delhi. The roads are very bad. I have relatives in UP and NCR cities like Ghaziabad and Noida. Modi govt has done a lot of development there. Once I enter Noida or Ghaziabad, the travelling is smooth, there are no huge traffic jams or potholes. AAP’s term is over now in Delhi.”

“Kejriwal has done a lot for schools, health by setting up mohalla clinics, free electricity for 200 units. The Centre has also done some work. We have ration cards. But because of the BJP, bade logon ko zyada faida huan (Rich people have benefited more). This time all the parties have promised many welfare schemes and guarantees. Kejriwal has already done so much. Not only here, public transport buses are free in Punjab as well. Every party has assured something or the other. I was constantly on Youtube.  Modi-saab nai kaha hein free buses sabhi states mein karenge, patah nahi jhooth hein ya phir sach. Meine youtube mein dhekha tha… Now it all depends on which party will work after coming to power. Kismat ki baat hein.”
Yuvraj Singh
Yuvraj Singh, 20, undergrad student, first-time voter

“Today, I am happy because I voted for the first time. I voted for BB Tyagi as I like him as a person and he is also a good candidate. I expect that he will provide better facilities in the area.”

Ritika Mishra, finance sector, Laxmi Nagar constituency

Encroachment ho raha hai roz, koi hata nahi raha hai… (New encroachments are cropping up everyday, yet nobody is there to remove them.)”

Suresh Kumar, senior citizen, Kalyanpuri (Kondli constituency)

headline: Why Mumbai’s STP project got lion’s share of funding in this year’s BMC budget
description: The sewage treatment plants at Worli, Bandra, Dharavi, Versova, Malad, Ghatkopar and Bhandup are expected to bridge the demand-supply gap of water supply in Mumbai.
content:
In its annual civic budget for the financial year 2025-26, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) allocated Rs 5,545 crore, which is 12.8 per cent of the entire capital expenditure, for constructing seven sewage treatment plants (STP) in Mumbai. This marks a 35 per cent jump in allocation as compared to last year.
With the overall cost pegged at over Rs 30,000 crore, the ground-breaking ceremony for this project was carried out by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in January 2023.
Here’s a look at why the STP project received a major chunk of funding in this year’s BMC budget.
What is the STP project?
An STP is a treatment facility that scientifically treats wastewater for potable and non-potable uses. The STP project being executed by the Mumbai Sewage Disposal Project (MSDP) department will see seven STPs being constructed across Mumbai with a collective capacity of treating 2,464 million litres (MLD) of water daily for potable usage. In addition to this, the STPs will have a combined capacity to treat 1,232 MLD of water further for non-potable use.
Where will these STPs come up?
The STPs are being constructed at seven locations in Mumbai – Worli, Bandra, Dharavi, Versova, Malad, Ghatkopar and Bhandup. Of these seven STPs, the largest one is located in Worli, which will have a capacity of treating 500 MLD of water, followed by Malad (454 MLD), Dharavi (418 MLD), Bandra (360 MLD), Ghatkopar (337 MLD), Bhandup (215 MLD) and Versova (180 MLD).
Why is the STP project important for Mumbai?
Being an island city, Mumbai does not have any natural resources to draw its water from. Daily, the BMC supplies 3,800 MLD of water to Mumbai which comes from seven different lakes, five of which are located in the satellite districts of Thane, Palghar and Nashik. Of the total water received, around 80 per cent or 3,040 MLD is converted into sewage or wastewater after usage. Also, the water that is supplied by the BMC has a shortfall of 400 MLD since Mumbai’s actual requirement is 4,250 MLD every day.
“Our problem is that Mumbai is used to throwing its entire sewage and wastewater into the sea that would go deep by about eight to 10 km. The overall volumetric sludge of sewage collected every day is equivalent to the size of Powai Lake,” Bhushan Gagrani, Municipal Commissioner and state-appointed administrator, said in an Idea Exchange organised by The Indian Express on January 21.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Therefore, in a bid to bridge the deficit of demand and supply, the BMC mooted the STP project so that it can recycle at least 2,464 MLD or 80 per cent of Mumbai’s daily sewage water and bring it back to the city for its potable usage, which in turn will bridge the deficit of daily water supply, leading to equal distribution of water.
What is the current status of each STP?
Of the seven STP projects, Bhandup, Ghatkopar and Dharavi are set to be operational by July 2026, while the facilities at Bandra, Versova and Worli are set to be operational by July 2027. The Malad facility is set to become operational by 2028.
According to the BMC’s budget document, the highest progress of completion of 28 per cent is recorded at Ghatkopar, followed by 26 per cent at Bhandup, 20 per cent each in Dharavi and Bandra, 18 per cent at Versova, 17 per cent at Worli and 7 per cent at Malad.
Abhijit Bangar, Additional Municipal Commissioner, Projects, who is spearheading this operation, told The Indian Express, “Of the various infrastructure projects that BMC has taken up, the STP project is running well on schedule. The civil works for the Malad facility could only begin in 2024 since the process of land acquisition and environment clearances took time. Yet in this short while, we have achieved significant progress.”
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
“Once they are ready, these STPs will not only bridge the demand-supply gap of water supply in Mumbai by a significant margin but also will contribute towards controlling water pollution as well,” Bangar added.

headline: ‘Chased my vehicle for over 4 km, fired 6 shots’: After ex-Punjab MLA Kulbir Singh Zira’s complaint, FIR lodged
description: Former Punjab Congress MLA Kulbir Singh Zira said that he had been threatened by the Arsh Dalla and Bambiha gangs in the past.
content:
Hours after former Punjab Congress MLA Kulbir Singh Zira lodged a complaint saying that some unidentified people had tailed his car and fired six shots at it while he was returning to his house in Zira in the state’s Ferozepur district on Monday night, the police lodged a First Information Report (FIR) late on Tuesday night.
The FIR was lodged against unknown persons on charges of reckless and negligent acts endangering the safety of others under Section 125 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and sections 25 and 27 of the Arms Act, the police said.
Zira, 44, is the president of the Ferozepur district Congress committee.
“Unknown persons chased my vehicle for over 4 km and fired six rounds at my vehicle on Monday night. I had informed the police the same day and got my statement recorded the next day, i.e. February 4,” Zira said in his complaint. “In the past, I have received threats from gangster Arsh Dalla and the Bambiha group as well. So, I want the police to act swiftly in this matter,” he added.
The FIR reveals that on Monday, Zira was returning home after attending a Kabaddi tournament function at Bootanwali village along with his personal assistant Akashdeep Rubal, Congress leader Dr Rashpal, and gunman Karnail Singh. While Zira was seated in the passenger seat, Rubal and Singh were seated in the back seat, as per the FIR.
“It was 6.30 pm when I started from Bootanwali village and later, I had a stopover at the house of Nambardar Amrik Singh in village Armanpur. At around 8.10 pm on Monday when we restarted, my driver told me that some vehicle was following us. So we briefly stopped in Sher Khan village and the vehicle following us also stopped. So we got suspicious…driver increased the speed of the vehicle and the following vehicle too increased its speed ..after about 1.5 km stretch, he fired two rounds at the vehicle which got misfired,” Zira told the police, as per the FIR.
“We hurriedly overtook a truck. The vehicle following us lost balance but continued following us and fired four more rounds and missed the target yet again. We reached Kulgari village by then and the vehicle disappeared,” he added.
Zira said he reached home and informed the police.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
“There were at least two people…could be more. Two rounds were fired from the passenger side in the front and four from the driver’s side,” Rubal said on Wednesday.
“Investigation is going on in the case and we have lodged the FIR,” Randhir Kumar, Superintendent of Police, Ferozepur district, said.
Zira became an MLA in 2017 in the Captain Amarinder Singh-led Congress government. In 2022, he lost to Aam Aadmi Party’s Rajesh Kataria. In 2024, he contested from the Khadoor Sahib Lok Sabha seat on a Congress ticket but lost to Independent candidate Amritpal Singh. His father Inderjit Singh Zira was a two-time Akali Dal MLA  and a former cabinet minister in the SAD-BJP government. Later, he and his son switched to Congress.

headline: Thief who gifted Rs 3-crore house to actress girlfriend arrested in Bengaluru: police
description: The 37-year-old man, who allegedly started stealing as a teen, was arrested over a burglary in Bengaluru.
content:
A 37-year-old Maharashtra man who has allegedly committed thefts in many parts of the country over the past two decades has been arrested in Bengaluru, B Dayananda, Commissioner of Police, said on Tuesday.
Panchakshari S Swamy, a native of Solapur, has been arrested in connection with the January 9 theft of gold and silver ornaments worth Rs 14 lakh from a house at Maruti Nagar in the Karnataka capital.
The police said they identified Swamy as the suspect after collecting footage from more than 200 CCTV cameras. They seized gold biscuits of 181 g, silver ornaments of 33 g, and a firearm from him.
According to a police officer, Swamy began committing burglaries in 2003, when he was a minor. By 2009, he had turned into a professional thief, amassing wealth worth crores. In 2014-15, he developed a romantic relationship with an actress and spent lavishly on her, building a Rs 3-crore house in Kolkata and gifting her an aquarium worth Rs 22 lakh.
In 2016, the Gujarat police arrested Swamy, resulting in a six-year term in Sabarmati Central Jail, Ahmedabad. After his release, he resumed burglaries, leading to another arrest, this time by the Maharashtra police. Following his release in 2024, he moved to Bengaluru, where he continued his criminal activities. There is a case against him in Belagavi also, according to the police.
A police officer involved in the investigation said, “He is a womaniser and has spent a lot of money on women. He has a wife and a child but has gifted a house valued at Rs 3 crore to his girlfriend in Kolkata. Most of the time he operates alone, watching empty houses and targeting them easily. He also holds a black belt in karate and has links with some actresses.”
After committing crimes, Swamy would frequently change clothes to avoid suspicion, the police said.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Swamy’s mother got a job in the railways after his father’s death, police sources said, adding that he had owned a house in his mother’s name and that a bank had issued an auction notice for the property over unpaid loans.

headline: Man who sent Mahakumbh threat used cook’s phone, arrested: Police
description: A statement from the GRP Tuesday said that a person had on February 1 allegedly sent a message on the helpline number of the Railway Protection Force (RPF) in Ahmedabad and Prayagraj.
content:
The Local Crime Branch (LCB) of the Government Railway Police (GRP) of the Western Railway (WR) Tuesday said it has arrested a man who used another man’s phone to issue threats of explosions at the ongoing Mahakumbh Mela, Ahmedabad railway station and the Ahmedabad airport.
The accused has been identified as Arunkumar Dineshchandra Joshi
A statement from the GRP Tuesday said that a person had on February 1 allegedly sent a message on the helpline number of the Railway Protection Force (RPF) in Ahmedabad and Prayagraj.
An FIR was filed at the GRP police station at Kalupur railway station in Ahmedabad.
The police initially zeroed in on one Faizal.
The SIM card used to send the threat message was registered in his name, they said. However, later, they found that Faizal was not the one who had actually sent the message.
The GRP statement revealed that Joshi had lent Faizal some money, which he had not been able to recover, and thus he had sent the message from Faizal’s number to harass him.
PI H K Shrimali of the LCB said, “Joshi owns a grocery shop in Gandhidham. Faizal, a cook at a firm in the city who used to purchase groceries on credit from Joshi, wasn’t able to clear some dues. When Joshi finally caught hold of Faizal, he sent the message from the latter’s phone. The browser history on Joshi’s phone also showed that he had searched for the helpline numbers of the RPF.”
However, the police also confirmed that Joshi actually had no intention to carry out the explosions, and just wanted to harass Faizal.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Joshi was booked under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) Sections 351(2)(3)(4) (criminal intimidation) and 353(2) (making, publishing, or circulating statements that create or promote enmity, hatred, or ill will between groups), said the police.

headline: UK Indian High Commission attack: Delhi court grants bail to British national, says ‘nothing could be shown he was part of conspiracy’
description: The UK national was arrested last year for his alleged involvement in the attacks on the Indian High Commission in London in March 2023.
content:
A Delhi Court recently granted bail to a UK national allegedly involved in an attack on the Indian High Commission in the United Kingdom in March 2023, noting that the National Investigation Agency (NIA) could not establish his link with the incident.
While granting bail to Inderpal Singh Gaba, the court asked him to surrender his passport and not leave the country without its permission.
“However, the NIA is unable to establish any link of the applicant (Gaba) with the incident of 19.03.2023. He was neither present at the spot nor was associated with arranging anything for the demonstration and for that matter, nothing could be shown that he was part of the conspiracy to organize the demonstration on 19.03.2023 or for that matter on 22.03.2023,” said Principal District and Sessions Judge Vimal Kumar Yadav of Patiala House Court in his order dated January 29.
Gaba was arrested by NIA in April last year for his alleged involvement with the violence by alleged Khalistani supporters at the Indian High Commission in London during a protest on March 22, 2023. The agency filed a chargesheet against Gaba on September 5, 2024, under Indian Penal Code sections 109 (abetment), 147(rioting), 148 (rioting with a deadly weapon), 149 (being part of an unlawful assembly), 120B (criminal conspiracy), and sections of the UAPA among others.
As per NIA, Gaba, a Sikh of Afghan origin, went to London in 1995, and started a grocery store there. He ran three stores called Strawberry Local Group in Greater London, the agency claimed.
NIA said the attacks on March 19 and March 22, 2023, by alleged Khalistani supporters were found to be in retaliation to the action taken by Punjab Police against pro-Khalistani separatist Amritpal Singh on March 18, 2023.
To drive home this point, the Central agency relied on audio clips allegedly shared on March 19, 2023, on a WhatsApp Group called Waris Punjab De UK. In these alleged audio clips, a person could be heard requesting the members of the group to “come at Park Avenue Gurudwara as the protest which is already scheduled, is on Wednesday (22.03.2023) which is far away”. The agency also relied on statements of eyewitnesses who allegedly said some common faces were present during both protests. CCTV footage, as per NIA, pointed to the same — that the two incidents were part of a larger conspiracy.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
“The nature of allegations against the applicant, if taken on its face value, then also the kind of offences, which are under the scope and ambit of the UAPA, could not be found so as to bring in the purview of Section 43 (D)(5) of UAPA,” the court noted in its order.
Section 43(D)(5) of the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act makes it virtually impossible to get bail.
Advocate Arun Khatri, who represented Gaba in Court, argued the only allegation against his client was that he was part of the protest on March 22, 2023, and that there was nothing against him except video footage in which he is allegedly seen vandalising the property of Indian High Commission during the protest. None of these allegations, he argued, could attract provisions of the UAPA.
Noting that Gaba wasn’t an Indian, Judge Kumar noted that, “his attachment towards India must not be that strong and sincere if at all it is there.” However, Judge Kumar cautioned that “this doesn’t permit him to do things which are anti-Indian”.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
“…no involvement in any act of violent nature has been alleged against the applicant/accused. All these factors when taken into consideration and the period of custody coupled with the age and the expected time to be taken in trial, then it appears that the trial, which has not commenced so far, would likely to take a very long time,” the Judge said. “In such circumstances, when there is no mechanism available with the human race to return time to anyone then how far it would be appropriate to keep a person under custody…,” he added.
NIA also alleged it had found an alleged photo of Gaba with an AK 47 assault rifle in his photo gallery. “…albeit no such rifle has been recovered, nor for that matter, it can be said conclusively, that it was an AK 47 rifle or a dummy. In this era of deepfake Photoshop, etc., there can’t be any certainty that what has been shown is correct. More so, it is not very uncommon that people pose for photographs with all kinds of stuff,” the Judge said.
The agency also said that a black car allegedly owned by Gaba had a number plate with “KHISTAN” written on it. The symbol on the number plate was that of Khalistan and the registration number had been chosen in such a fashion which reflected his association with “Khalistan”, alleged NIA.
“This in itself is not enough to attribute anything, which is unlawful. Even if it is presumed that the allegations are correct, still the applicant can’t be held criminally responsible for committing any offence. Such fancy numbers are permitted by the vehicle Registration Authority in the western part of the globe,” Judge Kumar noted.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
“It, however, definitely indicates towards the mindset of the applicant vis-a-vis Khalistan. The idea of Khalistan whereas in itself is questionable. Incidentally, it may be rather, it is against, in a way, each and every nation including the country where the accused was living. However, there was absence of any action against the applicant from the Government of the country where accused lived and worked…,” he added.

headline: PMC’s property tax defaulters include 59 Central and 287 state govt properties
description: In a statement, the PMC stated that there are 438 government-owned properties with pending dues of Rs 142 crore and steps are being initiated to recover the dues.
content:
Declaring a list of top 100 defaulters of property tax amounting to Rs 334.1 crore, the Pune Municipal Corporation (PMC) on Tuesday decided to intensify its drive to recover property tax from defaulters or seal the property and disconnect the water supply.

headline: ED attaches properties worth Rs 26.30 crore in Rs 139 crore cheating case
description: The properties include 24 immovable assets held in the names of Sunil Kumar Garg (ex-Managing Director), Nikhil Agarwal (ex-Finance Head), their family members, and associated firms, the ED revealed in a statement on Tuesday.
content:
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has provisionally attached immovable properties worth Rs 26.30 crore in connection with a Rs 139 crore cheating case under the provision of Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA).
The attached properties were acquired using proceeds from crime by former employees of M/s HUF India Pvt Ltd, a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Germany-based HUF Halswerk and Furst GMBH & Co. KG. The properties include 24 immovable assets held in the names of Sunil Kumar Garg (ex-Managing Director), Nikhil Agarwal (ex-Finance Head), their family members, and associated firms, the ED revealed in a statement on Tuesday.
The ED’s investigation stems from an FIR filed by Sandeep Jagdish Choudhary, Managing Director of HUF India Pvt Ltd, at Chakan Police Station. The FIR accuses ex-employees of defrauding the company of Rs 139 crore. The police have charged the accused under sections 420, 406, 409, 467, 468, 471, and 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
According to the ED, between 2010 and 2020, the former employees colluded to defraud HUF India Pvt Ltd. They manipulated purchase orders, created false invoices, and used a fake company stamp to generate goods receipt notes (GRNs). These actions allowed them to release funds to vendors without any goods or services being provided.
The vendors involved in the scam subsequently transferred the funds back to the bank accounts of Garg, Agarwal, their family members, and associated firms under the pretense of providing consultancy services, despite no such services being rendered. The accused also extorted commission payments from vendors, threatening to stop their services unless payments were made.
The illicit funds were transferred into personal and dummy firm accounts, which were then used to acquire movable and immovable properties in the names of Garg, Agarwal, their families, and the firms.
Earlier, on September 4, 2024, the ED conducted searches at the premises of the accused and vendors, freezing bank accounts, fixed deposits, shares, and mutual fund investments worth Rs 10.15 crore.

headline: BMC Junior Engineer exam: Candidates seek TCS iON as centre to avoid malpractices
description: The BMC’s October 2024 notification for 690 Junior and Sub Engineer positions in mechanical, electrical, and civil departments has sparked a debate as candidates found their exam centres allocated in remote locations rather than at Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) iON digital facilities.
content:
Candidates for the upcoming Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) engineering recruitment examinations are raising concerns about exam centre allocations, highlighting the balance between accessibility and examination integrity.
The BMC’s October 2024 notification for 690 Junior and Sub Engineer positions in mechanical, electrical, and civil departments has sparked a debate as candidates found their exam centres allocated in remote locations rather than at Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) iON digital facilities. With the mechanical and electrical engineering exams scheduled for February 9, students are demanding to address the concerns.
“We will face extra expenditure just to reach our allocated centres,” said Tushar Bhalchim, a mechanical engineering candidate from Pune who is assigned to a centre in Nashik. “Despite applying early, many of us will need to bear additional costs of around Rs 3,000 for travel and accommodation to reach far-flung locations like Bhandara and Nagpur. We demand that BMC should verify the centre choice before allocation.”
“The Water Conservation Department (WCD) and Town Planning Assistant (TPA) examinations held in 2024 at these remotely located centres were cancelled due to copying and malpractices, and an FIR was lodged against the centre. But the centre has been renamed and candidates have been allotted the same centres. We doubt that a similar copying case could be repeated due to the lack of high-end security facilities,” said Gaurav Daga, an Amravati-based aspirant.
“TCS iON’s digital zones offer significant advantages, including real-time anomaly detection and sophisticated image processing algorithms to identify malpractices. These features are notably absent in the currently allocated Industrial Training Institutes (ITI), MSCIT centres and others,” said Ramesh Bhutekar, chairman of the Municipal Engineers Association, Mumbai.
“We urge both BMC and The Institute of Banking Personnel Selection (IBPS), an autonomous body, which will conduct the exam on behalf of BMC to reconsider their centre allocation and to shift all examinations to the TCS iON digital zone to safeguard the integrity and transparency of the examination,” Bhutekar added.
“We are going to provide additional police force to deter any cheating incidents, but as the exam is approaching soon, we won’t be able to shift the centres. However, students’ demand for iON digital centres and allocation to preferred choices may be considered for the civil engineering exam scheduled in March after consultation,” said Mahendra Ubale, city engineer, BMC.

headline: Need to expand use of space-based tech to mitigate climate change, disease outbreaks and disaster: study
description: Citing recent outbreaks of Ebola and Covid involving animal-to-human virus transmission, the study underscores contributory environmental factors like deforestation, urbanisation, and climate change that need monitoring using space-based tools.
content:
As India gears up for the big-ticket satellite mission NISAR (Nasa-Isro Synthetic Aperture Radar), an international study has advocated enhanced use of space-based tools and technologies to tackle climate change, health issues, and disasters.
Expected to launch from Sriharikota in March, NISAR will be positioned in low Earth orbit. It will be the first Earth-observing satellite equipped with two kinds of radars designed to map the globe once every twelve days and provide spatio-temporal data. The mission aims to offer a better understanding of changes in Earth’s ecosystems, the poles, deformation, and cryosphere by observing sea levels and shorelines, sea ice mass, and its characteristics, vegetation, groundwater and more.
“Often, people connect space to only space exploration and are less aware of how space technology can help address Earth-based issues. Once health and environmental experts share the key information needed to monitor, mitigate or even prevent crises, then the space sector can aim to provide the relevant data by incorporating the data collection into future space missions/satellites,” Dr Farhan Asrar, an associate professor at the University of Toronto, told The Indian Express in an email reply.
With Earth becoming a hotter place owing to climate change, information about land surface temperature, vegetation and precipitation could be crucial in tackling vector-borne diseases or outbreaks, including pandemics like Covid, the researchers said.

Asrar, along with co-author Helena Chapman, representing Nasa, has urged health professionals and environmentalists to adopt the concept of One Health — human-animal-environment.
