For the experiential part of the tour, a medium-sized excavation pit has been created inside the museum. Here, visitors are encouraged to use the available archaeological tools “to excavate real objects”, besides trying their hands on the mortar and pestle, and the miniature stone grinder.
The actual excavated site that is connected with the museum through a walkway for visitors. (Express photo by Bhupendra)Rana
Besides replicas of marker coins recovered from the excavated site, which can be traced on paper with pencils, visitors can also use clay and moulds to make their own terracotta pots and watch them bake digitally. The museum also has activities for children. At a wall section, they can create paintings using watercolours and fill line drawings; in the shell gallery section, they can solve a jigsaw puzzle; they can also design their own bangles on a digital screen and feel them “digitally” on their hand; and they can also use large replicas of beads made of stone, glass and terracotta to make their own necklaces, among other activities.
“Integrated with an experiential walkway over the in situ excavation site, this is the first-of-its-kind museum in India. The thought behind it was to make someone visiting Vadnagar understand the history and importance of this town, which is over 2,500 years old,” Pankaj Sharma, director, Directorate of Archaeology and Museums, Gujarat, tells The Indian Express.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
To recreate the history of Vadnagar, the museum has 500 spots with audio guide sensors, eight main films, 30 sub films and various audio-visual galleries.
The remains of an actual fort wall are a part of the Vadnagar museum. (Express photo by Bhupendra Rana)
Director Sharma adds, “Using display and technology, the museum attempts to provide an exploration of the city’s evolution through interpretations of events over time. This includes examining practices like water management, the belief in the region being a sacred space and the significant role of Nagar Brahmins, among others.”
Galleries and experiences
While replicas help showcase the city’s evolution, over 6,000 real artifacts have also been displayed in the museum’s galleries.
“The representation of cultural periods (at the museum) involves illustrating various aspects, such as urban lifestyles, beliefs, political situations, social structure and noteworthy events, as gleaned from archaeological and historical discoveries. Excavated artefacts, epigraphic evidence, existing monuments and built environments serve as narrative elements too. The city’s ongoing growth and transformation are conveyed through horizontally stacked layers, with artefacts at the core of the curation process,” says Grace Ann Varkey, superintending archaeologist, Gandhinagar, and the museum’s curator incharge.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
The museum has seven galleries and experiences based on thematic frameworks: Reception and Orientation Gallery, Introduction Gallery, City Gallery, Belief Gallery, Lifestyle and Economic Gallery, Future Gallery and Introduction to Excavation Gallery.
The Introduction Gallery starts with a 270-degree projection show. The screen then opens — like a door — taking visitors to the next level, which has been designed to help them understand artefact highlights in relation to India and Gujarat. At the City Gallery, visitors experience a chronological narrative portraying the development of Vadnagar and its evolution via artefacts, replicas, installations, artworks, water management systems, streets, walls, excavation sites, monuments and more.
The remains of an actual fort wall are a part of the Vadnagar museum. (Express photo by Bhupendra Rana)
The excavated site gallery is dedicated solely to the Amba Ghat excavations, where a part of the actual dig has been recreated for visitors. The Belief Systems Gallery narrates the town’s religious landscape, including Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Islam, through related artefacts, rituals and existing religious structures. The Lifestyle and Economy Gallery depicts the town’s lifestyle, economic and trade activities, and their evolution over 2,500 years. This gallery includes subsections on agriculture practices, animal husbandry, pottery and technology evolution, global trade linkages and coin, terracotta, shell, glass, stone and ivory objects.
“These sections offer visitors immersive experiences, which include a variety of installations, artefacts, replicas, live workshops, 3D projections, set-ups based on AR and VR (augmented reality and virtual reality) and interactive installations,” says museum curator incharge Varkey.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
A diorama showcasing the history of Vadnagar in different galleries. (Express photo by Bhupendra Rana)
The Introduction to Excavation Gallery establishes the context of the excavation site by using a 3-D scaled model of the dig and installations on key findings. The gallery also introduces visitors to archaeological processes, tools and techniques.
The museum also includes three polished steel sculptures by Vibhor Sogani, an Indian artist and designer known for his large-scale public art installations. While one of these sculptures is inside the museum, two others have been installed in the gardens.
Talking about the remaining galleries, Siddha Shah, superintending archaeologist, Rajkot, says, “The Future Gallery contemplates the future of Vadnagar by emphasising our traditional knowledge systems, resilient practices, and the significance of our present actions in the context of future times and generations. Marking the conclusion of the museum experience, visitors are encouraged to contribute to building a wall, both digitally and physically.”

headline: 7 held for kidnapping doctor in Karnataka’s Ballari

content:

headline: ED claims CA Amber Dalal used fraudulently earned money to buy property near Burj Khalifa in Dubai
description: ED has claimed Amber Dalal operated a Ponzi scheme, where only a small percentage of the investors’ funds were used for investment or trading
content:
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has claimed that chartered accountant Amber Dalal, arrested in an alleged investment fraud, used investors’ money to cover losses incurred by him in stock market trading, paying credit card bills, and buying properties, including one in Dubai near Burj Khalifa.
Dalal was arrested on November 27, 2024, by ED following his arrest in March 2024 by the Mumbai police. ED has claimed that Dalal operated a Ponzi scheme, where only a small percentage of the investors’ funds were used for investment or trading and old investors were being paid using funds from new investments.
Earlier this month, ED filed its prosecution complaint (chargesheet) against Dalal and an acquaintance Rashmi Prasad. The Central agency has claimed that the proceeds of crime in the case are to the tune of Rs 564 crore, layered in various bank accounts and entities belonging to Dalal or his family.

headline: Palace Land row: Karnataka issues ordinance to avoid paying over Rs 3,000 crore for road widening
description: The ordinance comes in the wake of a Supreme Court order in December last year to provide transferable development rights (TDR) to the erstwhile Mysuru royal family for 15 acres and 17 guntas of land sought to widen Ballari and Jayamahal Roads.
content:
The Karnataka government on Wednesday notified the Bangalore Palace (Utilization and Regulation of Land) Ordinance 2025, reserving the right to not acquire portions of the disputed Palace land located in the heart of the city. The ordinance is expected to jeopardise proposals to widen two major roads—Ballari Road and Jayamahal Road.
The ordinance came in the wake of a Supreme Court decision in December last year ordering the government to provide the erstwhile Mysuru royal family with transferable development rights (TDR) for 15 acres and 17 guntas of land sought to widen the two roads to reduce traffic congestion. The judgment estimated TDR for the land to be worth Rs 3,011 crore, as per the prevailing guidance value.
The ordinance said the “financial effect of the judgement of the Hon’ble Supreme Court will be grave on the exchequer of the state of Karnataka, and upon the urban planning of the city of Bengaluru”.
The Bangalore Palace (Acquisition and Transfer) Act 1996, which empowered the state government to acquire portions of the palace land for infrastructure development, had valued the entire land of 472 acres and 16 guntas at Rs 11 crore. Though the Act, enacted almost three decades ago, was upheld by the Karnataka High Court, its constitutional validity remains challenged in the Supreme Court.

Police said that Bisoi, along with three others – Lakhan Khalai, Prakash Meherna and Vipra Pradhan – had killed one Banshi Pradhan in a room in Maharana Pratap Nagar in Varachha area in 1994. A complaint under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) sections 307 (attempt to murder), 302 (murder), and 114 (abettor present when crime is committed) was lodged against all the four accused.
Police said Meherna was arrested by Surat police in 2021 while Vipra was nabbed in 2022. Khalai died a few years ago, they added.
Surat Crime Branch police inspector K I Modi said, “All the four accused are natives of Ganjam district. They were staying together in a single room and were working in a powerloom factory in Varachha. For some unknown reason, Vipra had a quarrel with Banshi who used to stay in another room on the premises. With the intention of taking revenge, Vipra went back to his room where, along with his roommates – Biso, Mehrna, and Khalai – he hatched a plan of murder. The four men stormed into Banshi’s room and attacked him with a knife. After the murder, all the four accused escaped from the city.”
Modi further said, “Bishoi told police that he stayed in different places in West Bengal and Odisha all these years and came to Surat a few months ago with his family comprising his wife and two sons. He thought Surat police would have forgotten all about the case and he could stay here peacefully now, working at a textile
factory.”

headline: Mumbaikars await 5 key aligned projects including green space even as Mumbai coastal road opens up
description: The first phase of the Mumbai Coastal Road Project has entered its final leg but work on the 70 hectares earmarked for promenades, gardens, cycling tracks etc is moving at a very slow pace.
content:
When the plans for the first phase of the Mumbai Coastal Road Project (MCRP) were charted, they came bearing an ambitious promise. For a space-starved city grappling with the loss of tree cover, the project to alleviate traffic along its north-south corridors envisaged an expansive open, green space along the metropolis’s landward side and seaside.
Of the 111 hectares of land reclaimed from the sea to develop the coastal swathes, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) earmarked 70 hectares to develop an open landscape encompassing green pockets, gardens, cycling tracks and amphitheatres. It also includes plans to develop a brand new Marine Drive-like 7.5-km long promenade along the city’s coast.
However, even as the first phase has entered its final leg ushering in respite for motorists, citizens are yet to walk through the open space.
While work on the massive open space is yet to take off as the BMC has not appointed an agency for the landscaping works, other promises like the development of bus bays and pedestrian underpasses also remain hanging in the air.
STORIES YOU MAY LIKE
Jack the Ripper: Has a DNA breakthrough finally unmasked the murderer who terrorised Victorian London?
Rahul insulted Shivaji Maharaj with post offering ‘sraddhanjali’: Shinde
Sagarika Ghatge reveals Zaheer Khan wouldn’t even talk to her, kept his distance till Angad Bedi stepped in: ‘He was told, she’s that kind of girl’
While BMC officials confirmed that the civic body is eyeing December end to complete most works, Mumbai’s wait for enhanced green cover on the landward side is here to stay — for at least two more years.
For experts like Alan Abraham, an architect and urban planner, the neglect of open spaces contradicts the Joint Technical Committee’s 2011 report, which argued that land reclamation from the sea would create much-needed open spaces for Mumbai.
Abraham told The Indian Express: “Even though the Coastal Road, open now for several months, caters exclusively to private cars, has anyone been able to walk on the promenade or enjoy the open space on the landward side? The road occupies just 18 per cent of reclaimed land, while 82 per cent designated for open spaces remains undeveloped. When making the case for reclamation, the Joint Technical Committee promised new open spaces. So why are they now being neglected?”
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
As the MCRP marks a significant landmark with the complete operation of the bowstring arch bridge, The Indian Express examines the status of the pending works.
Butterfly gardens, seating spaces
In the blueprint floated in March last year, the civic body proposed a massive plan encompassing a thick Miyawaki forest, cycling tracks, butterfly gardens and seating spaces, among others on the reserved 70 hectares land.
After the initial proposal drew flak from several quarters, including architects, the civic body invited suggestions and objections from citizens, which senior officials said have now been weaved into their revised plans.
However, nearly a year since, work on the development of the green space is yet to take off.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
On January 11 this year, the BMC invited an Expression of Interest (EoI) from private companies and voluntary organisations for the design, development and maintenance of the space. As per the plan, private entities will now take up the parcel for a specific period of time to develop and maintain the open space, while also bearing the costs for the same.
The proposition of private entities developing the open space too has now drawn concerns among citizens.
“The BMC spent Rs 14,000 crore of its own funds on the toll-free Coastal Road, which serves just 0.6 per cent of Mumbai’s population, yet it cannot spare Rs 400 crores—under 3 per cent of the project cost—for open spaces that benefit everyone. While the BMC has demonstrated its ability to fund big-ticket projects, why is it involving a private corporate when this land is meant for public use?” said Alan Abraham.
Meanwhile, according to Municipal Commissioner Bhushan Gagrani, the development of the 70-hectare parcel will be completed over the next two years.
A promenade by March?
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
The BMC is also developing a 7.5-km long promenade on the seaward side. Spanning from Breach Candy to Worli, the new promenade will comprise trees and offer a space where citizens can stroll and unwind. Furthermore, the BMC has also earmarked a separate cycle track along the upcoming promenade.
However, work on the project is still underway with senior officials stating that the promenade will be opened in entirety by March 2025.
“We are completing concreting works, installation of paver blocks and colour concreting for the cycling track,” an official said.
Last year, the BMC had also readied a mock-up of the promenade at Worli. Modelled after a Hong Kong-based concept, it had been developed with palm trees, decorative lights and seating pockets.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
However, officials hinted that several aspects from the mock-up patch have been dropped for the remaining stretch of the promenade owing to feasibility and technical challenges.
Only one of 20 pedestrian underpasses open
To enable pedestrians to cross from the open spaces on the landward side to the coast, the civic body had charted plans to develop 20 underpasses beneath the main thoroughfare.
Of the 20 pedestrian underpasses (PUP), 11 are situated across the main carriageway while nine are across interchange arms.
However, the civic body is yet to complete work on the underpasses. Currently, only one underpass – near the Haji Ali entry point to facilitate devotees visiting the shrine – has been opened. Last year in April, the BMC drew flak after its PUP at Haji Ali submerged under water.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
As per officials, granite laying and flooring works among others have already been executed with the civic body now completing roofing works. All the pedestrian passes are likely to be opened by May 2025.
Bus bays: Final work pending
While the coastal road has a dedicated bus lane, it has yet to get bus bays or even ferry BEST buses through it. The BMC has charted plans to develop 10 bus bays along the 10.5-km stretch between Marine Drive and Worli.
A senior civic official said that only street furniture, signages and other final works are pending on the development of the bus bays. However, its functionality is dependent on the clearance of the land parcel on the landward side.
Plans in place to beautify dividers
Even though the roads became functional in March 2024, the beautification works on the coastal road’s median were only kicked off on Sunday when the chief minister and other ministers performed a groundbreaking ceremony for the project by planting trees.
Encompassing an area of 4.83 hectares, Tata Sons Limited through its CSR funds carried out the beautification of the dividers from Priyadarshini Park to Worli. Nearly 4.35 km long, the greening works are likely to be completed over the next eight to nine months.
Parking lots: 2 nearing completion
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
To address Mumbai’s parking space crisis, the BMC also also proposed to create four new vehicle parking lots to cater to over 1,850 vehicles.
However, these facilities are yet to be opened to the public.
Dotting four locations along the coastal road — two at Worli, one at Haji Ali and another at Breach Candy (Tata Gardens) — senior officials said that all prerequisite permissions for the project had been procured in the coastal regulation zone (CRZ) plan.
Even as the civic body had already completed excavation, work on the two-storey underground parking lot for 246 cars at Breach Candy had been stalled since November owing to opposition from local residents over increased traffic density in the vicinity.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
After deliberations, the proposal was cancelled with senior civic officials stating that a fire brigade or a police chowki may now be developed in its stead.
Meanwhile, the plan for a parking lot at Lotus Jetty near Haji Ali was recently revised. The BMC will now develop a four-storey underground parking space for 1,069 cars as well as 70 buses.
According to officials, the two parking lots at Worli are nearing completion.
Each of these parking spaces is slated to accommodate over 200 vehicles. With only civil works pending now, these structures are likely to become operational over the next two months.

headline: Over 1.27 lakh applicants vie for 1,088 constable posts in Himachal

content:
The Himachal Pradesh Public Service Commission (HPPSC) has received 1.27 lakh (1,27,764) applications for 1,088 constable posts in the Himachal Pradesh Police. The recruitment process will begin with physical tests from February 6 across the state. The applicants include 88,202 men and 39,562 women, competing for 708 posts for men and 380 posts for women.
Sources said that while the minimum educational qualification required is Class 10+2, many applicants hold higher degrees, including M.Tech, B.Tech, master’s, and bachelor’s degrees. The application window was open from October 10, 2024, to December 31, 2024.
According to officials, the Physical Standard Test (PST) and Physical Efficiency Test (PET) will be conducted in all 12 districts, divided into three police ranges: North Range, South Range, and Central Range. The first PST/PET will take place at the Police Ground, 3rd Battalion Pandoh, in Mandi district on February 6, followed by Una district, where tests will be held at Police Lines Ground Jhalera on February 11. The final test is scheduled for March 27 at Mini Stadium Kalpa in Kinnaur district. Candidates who clear the PST and PET will qualify for the written examination.
An official said that female candidates would undergo testing first, followed by male candidates. All candidates must report to the test venues by 7 a.m. on their designated dates. headline: 7 killed, 50 injured as makeshift structure collapses at religious event in Baghpat
description: 11 police personnel among those injured; administration says organisers complied with all norms, orders probe.bagh
content:
At least seven people were killed and 50 others, including 11 police personnel, injured after a makeshift wooden structure collapsed during a Jain community event in Baraut town of Uttar Pradesh’s Baghpat district on Tuesday morning, police said.
The incident occurred at around 7.15 am in the campus of Digamber Jain Degree College where people had gathered to celebrate ‘Nirvana Laddu Parv’ of Bhagwan Adinath, the first Tirthankara of Jainism.
Those who died were identified as Tarashpal Jain, 75, Amit, 40, Usha, 65, Arun Jain, 48, Shilpi Jain, 25, Vipin, 44, and Kamlesh, 65, a police officer said.
“Of the injured people, 35 have been admitted to three hospitals in Baraut while some were referred to hospitals in Meerut and New Delhi. This is why it is difficult to estimate the exact number of the injured people,” Baghpat Additional District Magistrate (ADM) Manish Kumar said.
STORIES YOU MAY LIKE

British-Irish woman’s rape-murder in Goa: Behind the conviction that earned investigators a ‘thank you’
Seven people with serious injuries were in the intensive care unit (ICU) of Aastha Hospital in Baraut.
According to the police, there is a ritual of touching the feet of the first Tirthankara during the ‘Nirvana Laddu Parv’.
“When the devotees were going to touch the feet of the statue of the first Tirthankara, the stairs came down, leading to the collapse of the entire structure,” said Baraut Circle Officer Vijay Kumar Singh Tomar.
The administration has ordered an inquiry into the incident.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
“We are taking every possible measure to ensure the injured receive immediate and proper medical care. An inquiry has been ordered and those responsible will be dealt with sternly,” said Baghpat District Magistrate Asmita Lal.
Meanwhile, panic gripped the area after the incident resulted in a stampede-like situation. Police personnel were rushed to the scene to bring the situation under control, it is learnt.
“Though the organisers had complied with all norms, including obtaining permission, a probe has been ordered. It will find out what led to the collapse of the structure. Those found guilty will not be spared,” Baghpat the Superintendent of Police (SP) Arpit Vijayvargiya said.
Ashok Kumar Jain, vice president of Bhaktamar Prachar Sangathan, a wing of the Jain Samaj Samiti which holds the event annually, said, “The festival has been held at the same place since 1999 and a similar structure was erected .We had obtained a no-objection certificate and completed all formalities. But it appears that some wooden pillars supporting the structure were weak, leading to the accident.”
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
“We are in a deep shock today. The Chief Minister should announce a compensation of Rs 1 crore to the families of those who died and Rs 20 lakh to the injured. The victims need government support at this juncture,” said Amit Rai Jain, an office-bearer of the Jain Samaj Samiti.
Sanju Tomar, the head of the nursing staff at the Anand Hospital, Baraut, said, “Twenty injured persons were brought to our hospital in the morning. Three of them have been discharged. We still have 17 injured, a majority of them police personnel, including women.”
One of the injured police personnel, Kusum, 34, who was admitted to Anand Hospital, recounted the incident, “I along with two other women constables were deployed near the wooden staircases that went up to the statue of the 51-foot-high deity. The structure collapsed when there was a rush among devotees to outpace each other to touch the deity’s feet. I was trapped beneath the structure and fell on the ground after people started falling on us.”
Some eyewitnesses said the injured were taken to hospitals on e-rickshaws since the health facilities could not provide adequate ambulances on time. The death toll could rise further, they added.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Wasim, the contractor who has been erecting the wooden structure over the years, said, “Every year the event passes off peacefully without a single scratch to devotees. I am deeply upset over this as I am unable to figure out how this happened.”
Expressing his condolences on the deaths, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath directed the officials concerned to ensure proper medical treatment to the injured.

headline: Maha Kumbh: 10 cr pilgrims likely at Mauni Amavasya Amrit Snan today
description: AI-powered CCTV cameras and drones keeping eye on Mela area, say officials
content:
The Uttar Pradesh government has stepped up security as it gears up for the ‘Amrit Snan’ on ‘Mauni Amavasya’ on Wednesday, which is expected to draw around 10 crore pilgrims to the Maha Kumbh in just a day.
The Maha Kumbh 2025 has already witnessed over 15 crore pilgrims taking a holy dip in the past 17 days, the state government said on Tuesday.
Security measures have reached unprecedented levels for the day with deployment of personnel at every nook and turn along with installation of AI-powered CCTV cameras and drones keeping eye on the Mela area, spread over several hectares along the Triveni Sangam – the confluence of the Ganga, Yamuna and the mythical Saraswati.
While the Mela area has already been declared a no-vehicle zone for the next few days, the Prayagraj administration has also made a fervent appeal to local residents to avoid using four wheelers and opt for two wheelers only if carrying senior citizens to the Sangam. “Residents are requested to use two-wheelers or walk to facilitate the movement of pilgrims from across the globe,” District Magistrate Ravindra Kumar Mandar said.

According to the Uttar Pradesh government, on Makar Sankranti (January 14) alone, 3.5 crore devotees, saints, and Kalpwasis participated in the Amrit Snan. Over 45 lakh devotees had taken the holy dip by 8 AM on Tuesday, it added.

headline: No new GBS cases found, hospitals urged not to turn down patients
description: Scheme package announced for serious cases
content:
Pune Divisional Commissioner Chandrakant Pulkundwar has urged hospitals not to refuse patients with Guillain Barre Syndrome (GBS) due to high treatment costs. He said that the patients will be enrolled under the Mahatma Jyotiba Phule Jan Arogya Yojana (MJPJAY) scheme.

When contacted, Pulkundwar said there were no new cases reported and instructions to increase surveillance activities had already been carried out.
GBS is a rare but serious neurological disorder where the body’s immune system attacks the peripheral nerves. Treatment focuses on managing symptoms and preventing complications. These include treatments like plasma exchange (plasmapheresis)— where the procedure entails reducing nerve damage — and administering intravenous immunoglobulin, which pertains to introducing high doses of healthy antibodies in the body to block the harmful ones.

headline: ASER 2024: Percentage of 15 & 16-year-old boys in rural Gujarat not enrolled in school doubles since 2022
description: The ASER Rural India report also found that private school enrolment (age 6-14 years) has returned to pre-COVID levels in Gujarat.
content:
The percentage of boys aged 15-16 years old who are not enrolled in school has more than doubled in the last two years, as revealed by the Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) 2024 Gujarat Rural report released Tuesday. However, this increase is less among girls of the same age group.
The percentage of those not enrolled fell in Gujarat between 2018 and 2022, but increased in 2024. Almost 10 percent of boys and girls in this age group in the state are out of school.
In 2024, like in many other states, private school enrolment (age 6-14 years) has returned to pre-COVID levels in Gujarat. In 2018, enrolment in private schools was 12.4 per cent which declined to 8 per cent in 2022 and returned to 12.4 per cent in 2024.
Between 2022 and 2024, the percentage of 15-16-year-old boys not enrolled in schools has doubled from 4.2 per cent to 9.4 per cent. For girls, it went from 8 per cent to 10.5 per cent. In 2016, 18.7 of per cent boys and 23.5 per cent of girls were not enrolled in any school in the state. Notably, this includes both children who have never been enrolled and those who have dropped out.

The ASER Rural India report has been released after two years, after the last was published in 2022. Barring the newly formed districts, the remaining 26 districts in Gujarat were sampled using the Census 2011 frame across 780 villages, surveying 24,746 children in the age group of 3-16 years in the state. While 15,332 households in these 26 districts were covered, 648 government schools in these 780 villages were surveyed for the school infrastructure report.
The sampling selection process included 30 villages randomly selected in each district and 20 households randomly selected in each village.
From 2010 to 2024, the number of schools with an enrolment of 60 or less increased from 4.6 per cent to 14.4 per cent. In 2010, 623 schools were visited and in 2024, 648 schools were visited.

Also, in 2022, 17.2 per cent of children who are 3 years old were not in pre-school or school and, 8.1 per cent 4-year-old children were not in school. This has declined to 4.7 per cent in the 3-year age group and 3.8 per cent in 4-year-olds.
Reading and arithmetic levels
In rural Gujarat, there has been an increase of 10.7 per cent between 2022 and 2024 in reading levels of Class V children enrolled in government schools. On the other hand, math numbers have not changed much.
Pointing at recovery from the “learning loss” witnessed after the COVID pandemic among Class V children in government schools, in reading, 2024 figures are higher than in 2022.
Only 14.3 per cent of Class V students can solve Class II 3-digit by 1-digit division problems, while 46.3 per cent of the students can read at a Class II level.

Further, among Class VIII students, reading levels have increased since 2022, surpassing the pre-COVID levels — from 52.4 to 75.8 per cent. Arithmetic levels declined from 31.8 to 30.3 per cent.
Digital literacy
Despite Gujarat having a higher percentage of adolescents aged between 14-16 years with access to smartphones than the national level — 96 per cent against 89 per cent — it has a far less percentage of ownership. Against 31.4 per cent of adolescents across the country with ownership of smartphones, only 18.6 per cent of them in Gujarat have their own phones.
In rural Gujarat, 12.9 per cent girls aged 14-16 years old have their own smartphones against 24.6 per cent boys.
School infrastructure
Over half of Class I children — 59.8 per cent — were seen sitting with other classes, while 55.3 per cent of Class II children were also observed sitting with other classes in the classroom.

Libraries were not there at 16.4 per cent schools, and 28.2 percent of them had a library that children aren’t using. Meanwhile, 25.4 per cent schools lacked computers while 34.6 percent schools had them without children being able to access them.

headline: Traffic to be allowed in Bengaluru’s Cubbon Park on second and fourth Saturdays for 3 hours
description: Environmentalists and a section of Bengaluru residents have launched an online petition titled Cubbon Park Pradakshiney Haaki, demanding the space remain traffic-free on holidays.
content:
The Karnataka government has decided to allow vehicular traffic inside Bengaluru’s Cubbon Park from 7 pm to 10 pm on the second and fourth Saturdays. The 197-acre park is usually closed to vehicles on these days and Sundays to protect its biodiversity.
However, after much deliberation by the Bengaluru traffic police department, the government convened a meeting involving Chief Secretary Shalini Rajaneesh, officials from the Cubbon Park Conservation Committee, the traffic department, Shivajinagar MLA Rizwan Arshad and Shantinagar MLA N A Haris over the issue on January 21.
M N Anucheth, Joint Commissioner of Police (Traffic), said the opening of the park for traffic on all days would decongest traffic around the central business district and enhance accessibility for people travelling from the south to the north side of Bengaluru.
He also argued that traffic congestion caused by the closure on the second and fourth Saturdays is increasing pollution levels around Cubbon Park.

headline: Know Your City: A look at early years of water supply in modern Bengaluru
description: Historian Fazlul Hasan notes that in mid-1800s, a water bearer would draw from tanks and deliver it in leather bags in Bengaluru city and later Miller's Tanks were built to store more water around 1873.
content:
Water continues to be a longstanding worry in Bengaluru – either in the form of floods or when the water supply to homes runs out.
But historical records attest to the fact the conundrum of providing seamless supply of uncontaminated water in the region has been there at least since the mid-1800s, during the British era.
British government records show that as early as 1844, the local cavalry units were having problems at Ulsoor Lake, with horses having fallen ill after drinking the water, followed by drought and famine in 1875.
In the very earliest years of the city’s history under Kempe Gowda, the father of modern Bengaluru, it was a fortified town with hinterlands and villages well supplied by rivers such as the Vrishabhavathi and the innumerable lakes, ponds and tanks of the region. But as the locality became the centre of British administration in the region, the area’s population began to grow rapidly, putting pressure on water sources and increasing the possibility of contamination.
STORIES YOU MAY LIKE

Gold medallist female power-lifter dies after 270-kg barbell falls on neck during practice in Bikaner
Sagarika Ghatge reveals Zaheer Khan wouldn’t even talk to her, kept his distance till Angad Bedi stepped in: ‘He was told, she’s that kind of girl’
Just two decades after the 1844 incident, officials were noting that sewage flowing into the Ulsoor lake was still a problem.
The city was rapidly growing more congested – something that would become painfully apparent at the turn of the 20th century with the outbreak of plague.
Historian Fazlul Hasan noted in his book ‘Bangalore Through The Centuries’ that around the mid-1800s, the city was still operating under the ‘karanjee’ system in many areas, in which a water bearer would draw from the Dharmambudi and Sampangi tanks, delivering water in leather bags. As this and other sources proved increasingly insufficient, a series of tanks known as the Miller’s Tanks were built to store more water around 1873.
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
A famine and drought lasting for two years that struck the area in 1875 proved the inadequacy of these measures too. Close on the heels of this disaster, Colonel (later General) Richard Sankey worked on what is today known as the Sankey Tank, two years after his service in the second Anglo Afghan War. While this might have eased supply issues to a degree, water quality was still a major concern.
Malleswaram’s Bangaluru Water Supply and Sewerage Board (BWSSB) premises still houses a remnant of the filtration infrastructure of the times – the tanks which contained the Jewell Filters.
Fazlul Hasan quotes a local resident speaking to the visiting Governor of Madras, “The men who are thrown off their horses and killed….are the only ones that are allowed by doctors not to have died from drinking bad water.”
The next major initiatives to secure the city’s water supply were notably undertaken by authorities of the Mysore princely state – notably with the involvement of figures such as Sir M Visvesvaraya and Dewan K Seshadri Iyer, with water supply from the Hesaraghatta reservoir commencing in 1896. But with increasing connectivity, the city’s population was still growing exponentially – and the need for more water was underlined by yet another drought that broke out in 1925.
In the wake of this, the supply of water from the Tippagondanahalli (or TG Halli for short) reservoir was initiated in 1933. At the time, it was hailed as an example of Mysore’s self-sufficiency. As the then king Nalwadi Krishnaraja Wodeyar had said, ” The scheme has been worked from first to last…….by Mysore Engineers ….it is using not only Mysore water and Mysore brains but Mysore power and Mysore pipes.”
STORY CONTINUES BELOW THIS AD
Interestingly, Malleswaram’s Bangaluru Water Supply and Sewerage Board (BWSSB) premises still houses a remnant of the filtration infrastructure of the times – the tanks which contained the Jewell Filters. These were gravity-based sand filtration systems that replaced the earlier sand-bed filters which were prone to being clogged by algal growth. At the time, these were responsible for filtering the initial inflow of water from Hesaraghatta and TG Halli.

headline: Only 23% of Class 3 govt school students in Karnataka can do subtraction: ASER 2024 report
description: Karnataka has witnessed a decline in enrollment figures for children aged 6-14 in government schools, dropping from 76 per cent in 2022 to 71 per cent in 2024.
content:
Only 23 per cent of Class 3 students in Karnataka government schools are able to perform numerical subtraction, according to the Annual Status of Education Report (ASER) 2024 released on Tuesday. Although this figure has improved from 19 per cent in 2022, it has only increased by 2 per cent over the past 10 years. In comparison, 31 per cent of Class 3 students in private schools in Karnataka can perform numerical subtraction, indicating slightly better performance, as per the report.
ASER is an annual citizen-led survey that provides reliable estimates of children’s schooling and learning levels. The report also showed that only 19 per cent of government school students in Class 5 and 35 per cent in Class 8 can do division, as compared to 25 per cent and 43 per cent, respectively, in private schools.
According to ASER, Karnataka has witnessed a decline in enrollment figures for children aged 6-14 in government schools, dropping from 76 per cent in 2022 to 71 per cent in 2024. However, this figure is still higher compared to 2018, when the enrollment rate was 69 per cent. Additionally, 83 per cent of government primary schools in Karnataka have fewer than 60 students, and 22 per cent of upper primary or higher schools also have fewer than 60 students. This, however, represents an increase of 17 per cent from 2022.
Among 4-year-olds, enrollment in pre-primary institutions in India increased from 76 per cent in 2018 to 82 per cent in 2022 and 83.3 per cent in 2024. In Karnataka, the enrollment rate for this age group exceeded 95 per cent. Additionally, there were significant increases in enrollment among 5-year-olds, with the rate in Karnataka surpassing 90 per cent.

headline: When Field Marshal KM Cariappa ticked off Nehru for not replying to his letters
description: On the 125th birth anniversary of K M Cariappa, here’s a look at one of his letters to Jawaharlal Nehru.
content:
Field Marshal K M Cariappa, the first Indian Commander-in-Chief of the Army, wrote a series of letters to then Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru with several suggestions — from the Kashmir issue to the setting up of a National Defence College.
After his retirement, Field Marshal (then General) Cariappa served as the high commissioner of India to Australia and New Zealand from 1953 to 1956 and after completing this tenure he settled in Madikeri in Coorg.
On the 125th birth anniversary of K M Cariappa on January 28, here is a look at one of his letters to Jawaharlal Nehru.
In his letter dated April 14, 1960, a plain-speaking Cariappa expressed his annoyance to Nehru for not replying to two of his letters. “Since we last met on 16th January at Bangalore I have written to you two letters on matters which I thought and still think are of some importance. Taking you at your own word I have always written and talked to you quite frankly, without beating around the bush with no ulterior motives or political ambitions of any kind whatsoever. I know what a very busy person you are. But I did expect at least a line or two In reply to those letters. Have I said anything, traitorous or unpatriotic? At any time that you should so totally ignore the matters. I have written to you. Panditji, I never expected this of you. This is indeed a sad and tragic ‘discovery’ for me. I am afraid, I cause and create unhappiness to myself By being too much of an idealist,” wrote Cariappa.

Cariappa then went on to raise three issues in his letter which he had mentioned on previous occasions to Nehru. He referred to the urgent need to look into the morale of officers in the Army, and also opposed the setting up of a National Defence College citing expenses and administrative issues about it.
Field Marshal Cariappa also emphasised to Nehru the need to reach out to the then president of Pakistan Ayub Khan and solve the Kashmir issue, saying that it should not be left pending for future generations. “Panditji please do this in your lifetime. We cannot live forever and we cannot hold office forever. Ayub will be prepared to discuss things with you if you show your desire to thrash out the matter between you two. Please let India and Pakistan settle the 12-year-old matter between themselves. This will then secure a more permanent feeling of goodwill between the two countries than if it were left to someone else — third party to settle it for us,” he said.
Urging Nehru to give “a kind and charitable thought” to his suggestions, Cariappa ended the letter by asking Nehru not to dismiss his suggestions by saying “yet another irresponsible thing from one who is mental”.

Following raids at over 30 locations, including Gujarat, the Chennai Zonal Office of the Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Monday said it has arrested two masterminds in connection with an alleged countrywide digital arrest scam. While one suspect was apprehended in Kolkata, the second was arrested in Delhi while he was attempting to flee the country, the Central agency added.
Both suspects played a key role in managing mule accounts, converting illicit cash into cryptocurrency, and transferring it overseas, it said.
In its statement Monday, the ED said it had previously conducted raids at over 30 locations across West Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, and Maharashtra. During the searches, multiple mobile phones, laptops, and other electronic devices containing substantial incriminating evidence were seized. Cryptocurrency in the form of BTC (Bitcoin) and USDT (Tether, a form of cryptocurrency) was also found and seized.
The case stems from an FIR earlier filed by a senior citizen with the Chennai Police, alleging that scamsters defrauded her of Rs 33 lakh. The victim was allegedly threatened with fake allegations and the prospect of a “digital arrest”. ED investigation uncovered a network of layered mule bank accounts used to route fraudulent funds, the agency said. ED investigation revealed a sophisticated system wherein cash withdrawn from mule accounts was converted into cryptocurrency and transferred to entities suspected to be based abroad. Significant amounts of funds, originating from various digital fraud schemes, were routed through this method.
Additionally, the accused misused Cash Deposit Machines (CDMs) to deposit cash into the bank accounts of companies offering fintech services. These funds were then routed to individual accounts, enabling the accused to obtain cryptocurrency, the ED said. This cryptocurrency was allegedly used to conceal and transfer the Proceeds of Crime abroad with the assistance of accomplices using foreign phone numbers, it added.
